opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot. Right now, a lot of what makes ShinkaEvolve work well is still the human in the loop. We pick the evaluation function, we decide what the seed program looks like, and we set the mutation operators and the mix of language models. So in some sense the choice of optimization approach is still being made by us, the researchers.

But I think there's a really natural path toward the system making more of those decisions itself. The evolutionary loop is already a kind of meta-optimizer. The LLMs propose code changes, and those changes don't have to be small local tweaks to a heuristic. They can be "let's swap this greedy search for simulated annealing," or "let's try a gradient-based refinement step here." So in principle the program being evolved can itself discover which optimization paradigm fits the problem. We've seen glimpses of that, where the system stumbles onto a structurally different approach, not just a better-tuned version of the original one.

The other piece is adaptivity at the level of the search process itself. In ShinkaEvolve we already use something like a bandit over which LLM to query, based on which models have been producing improvements. You could extend that idea: a bandit or a learned policy over search strategies, over how much to exploit versus explore, over when to do a full rewrite versus a small diff. The system observes what's producing fitness gains and reallocates compute accordingly.

Where it gets really interesting, and harder, is transfer. Ideally you'd want a system that has seen many problems and builds up something like intuition: "This looks like a combinatorial packing problem, and last time local search with restarts did well, so let's start there." That's a kind of memory or meta-learning across runs, and I think that's where a lot of the open-endedness research is heading. You're not just solving one problem, you're accumulating a library of stepping stones and strategies.

I'd be a bit cautious, though. The evaluation function is still doing a lot of heavy lifting. If your fitness signal is noisy or easy to game, the system will happily pick the "optimization approach" that exploits the evaluator rather than solving the problem. So I think for the foreseeable future, the most productive setup is a collaboration: humans define what good looks like, and the system gets increasing freedom over how to get there.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we thought about a lot while building ShinkaEvolve, because I think the honest answer is that there isn't a single "right" optimization approach, and a system that pretends there is will fall over the moment you hand it a problem that doesn't look like the one you designed it for.

The way I like to frame it is that evolutionary program search is really a sequence of decisions under uncertainty. At every step you're deciding which parent to mutate, how aggressive the mutation should be, which model to ask, and how much of your budget you're willing to spend on exploring versus exploiting what already works. And the right answer to each of those depends on where you are in the search. Early on, when you know very little about the fitness landscape, you want diversity, you want to be trying structurally different ideas. Later, when you've found a promising basin, you want to be making careful, local refinements. So the "right optimization approach" is not a property of the problem alone, it's a property of the problem and the current state of the search.

What we did in ShinkaEvolve was essentially stop hardcoding those choices and instead let the system adapt them from feedback. The clearest example is the LLM ensemble. We don't pick one model up front. We treat the set of models as arms of a bandit and we track, for each one, how often its proposals actually lead to fitness improvements on this particular task. Some models are great at bold rewrites, some are better at small careful edits, and crucially, which one is more useful shifts over the course of a run. So the system allocates more calls to whichever is paying off right now, and that allocation keeps updating. The same spirit applies to parent selection, where we balance exploitation of high-fitness programs against novelty, so that you don't collapse onto one lineage too early.

The other piece I'd emphasize is sample efficiency, because that's what actually makes this practical. Earlier systems in this space would happily burn thousands of evaluations, and in that regime you can be fairly sloppy about strategy because brute force covers for you. We wanted to get to the point where you can find something genuinely new with, say, a couple hundred samples. And once you're in that regime, every wasted evaluation hurts, so things like novelty-based rejection sampling become important. If a proposed child is semantically almost identical to something you've already evaluated, you reject it before paying the evaluation cost. That's a form of choosing your optimization approach too, it's deciding not to spend compute on a direction that won't teach you anything.

Where I think this goes next is that the meta-level itself should be learned. Right now the adaptation we do is fairly principled but still hand-designed, bandits with particular reward signals, particular novelty thresholds. The more interesting version is a system that looks at a new problem, recognizes something about its structure, whether it's a combinatorial optimization task, a scientific code, a tricky agent scaffold, and uses that to warm-start its search strategy from experience with related problems. Essentially evolving the evolver. We're not fully there, but I think that's the direction, and I think it's one of the places where open-sourcing the framework matters, because you get a much wider range of problems to learn that meta-knowledge from than any single lab would generate on its own.

astra-6.text:
I think you can frame that as a learning problem in itself. Rather than committing to one optimization approach upfront, the system could try a few approaches with a small budget and use the feedback to decide where to invest more computation.

The tricky part is defining what “right” means. Is it the method that improves the solution fastest, the one that finds the best solution eventually, or the one that’s most reliable across runs? Those objectives can lead to different choices.

You could also use experience from previous problems to inform that initial allocation. But I’d want the system to keep testing those assumptions against the actual problem. An approach that looks promising based on past experience might turn out to be a poor fit. So I’d think of it as a continual loop of proposing, evaluating, and reallocating resources, rather than a single decision about which optimizer to use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that choosing the optimizer is itself an optimization problem. You could give a system like Shinka Evolve access to a few different approaches—gradient-based methods, evolutionary search, perhaps a Bayesian optimization routine—and let it run small experiments to work out what’s useful for the particular task.

If you have reliable gradients, that’s a very strong signal to exploit them. If you’re searching over programs or discrete structures, you might need a different approach. And often the best solution is a combination: evolution explores the structure, while a gradient-based method tunes parameters within that structure.

The crucial part is the feedback loop. Can the system measure progress relative to the compute it’s spending, and use that feedback to change its strategy? Then you don’t need it to identify the perfect optimizer upfront. You need it to make a reasonable initial choice, test that choice, and adapt as it learns more about the problem.
